title: Which hidden radar / laser detector, and what the cluster shows
ask: Which concealed radar and laser detector goes in the car, and how much of its alert should the cluster show?
why: You ruled a speed-trap detector with nothing on the windshield, the sensors put where they work best and hidden, and only a warning on the cluster (D-383). Two kinds of product can do that, and they differ in cost and in what the cluster can show. A custom-install system (Escort's MAX Ci 360c / Redline Ci 360c class) comes as separate front and rear radar receivers and laser sensors made to hide behind the bumpers, about $2,000–4,000 and usually sold through installers. Its data link is not published, so the DCU could only read its alert output: the cluster could say RADAR or LASER, but not the band or the direction reliably. A Valentine One is the only detector with a published data link (its ESP bus: band, direction, strength, everything the cluster frame 0x320 carries), about $500, but it is one box with its antennas inside. Hiding it means mounting the whole unit behind a plastic panel with a view ahead. Radar passes through plain plastic, but its laser sensor needs a clear view, so laser detection would suffer. Some custom systems also sell laser "shifters" (jammers); those are illegal in many states and are not part of either option. Detectors themselves are illegal in Virginia and Washington DC. The bumpers are now being replaced and painted body colour (04-beauty, D-425): metallic paint blocks 24 GHz radar (V-061), so hidden radar sensors behind a painted bumper need an unpainted or non-metallic window in it - 04-beauty block 04.13 carries this.
options:
(a) A custom-install concealed system (Escort MAX Ci 360c class): front and rear sensors hidden in the bumpers. The DCU reads its alert output, and the cluster shows the alert and whatever the output tells it (at least radar vs laser). About $2,000–4,000. Cluster detail is limited to what its outputs give.
(b) A Valentine One hidden behind a panel with a forward view, on its published ESP link into the DCU. Full band, direction and strength on the cluster. About $500. Laser detection is weaker hidden, and it is one box, not separate sensors.
(c) Decide later. Nothing is bought; the radar pass-throughs stay capped.
recommend: (a), because it is the only one that matches "sensors in useful places, nothing visible"; (b) if full detail on the cluster matters more than hidden laser sensors.
stops: The detector's design (Z-002) and its harness pass-through (L3-RDR / L4-RDR). Nothing else.

title: How the stereo becomes 5.1 (the upmix)
ask: Should the stereo-to-5.1 upmix be (a) built by us in front of a current DSP-amplifier, (b) just the centre extraction a current DSP-amplifier has, or (c) a used JBL MS-8 with Logic7?
why: It decides what the amplifier is and whether there is a box of our own in the signal chain. You asked for an upmix like your home receiver's Dolby Pro Logic II Music mode: either in the amp, or home-built with no loss. No car amplifier or DSP sold today has Pro Logic II or anything like it. The last ones (JBL MS-8 with Harman Logic7, Alpine H700/H701/H800) are discontinued, because the car-audio makers won't pay Dolby's licence. So the choice is between building the upmix, buying an old unit that has one, or settling for what current DSP-amps do: pull a centre out of the stereo (Helix RealCenter) and feed the rears the left-minus-right difference. That gives a real centre but not a Pro Logic II-style surround.
options:
(a) Home-built upmix feeding a current multichannel DSP-amplifier digitally: a small processor we build (the head unit's front pair in, a Pro Logic II-style matrix or a newer upmix algorithm, 6 channels out over a digital link into the DSP-amp's digital input). No extra conversion beyond the one the DSP-amp already does, and we control the algorithm. Costs a board or small computer (about $60-200) plus build and tuning time; it becomes firmware we maintain. Keeps everything open.
(b) A current DSP-amplifier alone (Helix-class, with RealCenter and a differential rear fill): off the shelf, warranty, strong centre imaging; the surrounds only get the L-R difference, not a steered Pro Logic II mix. About $800-2000 for the DSP-amp. (a) can still be added later in front of it.
(c) A used JBL MS-8 (Logic7 upmix, a real car unit) in front of the amplifiers: the closest thing to Pro Logic II ever sold for cars, but discontinued years ago, used only, no support, 8 channels at 1990s-2010s DSP quality, and a unit that has to be found.
recommend: (a), unless you'd rather not own upmix firmware; then (b), which (a) can still be added in front of later
stops: The amplifier and upmix parts round (X-012, parts LP56 and LP57); the head unit and speaker round (X-011) goes ahead without it

title: What the panel's keys look like
ask: What style should the nine keys and four knobs on the new centre-stack panel be: factory-style caps in a faceplate, round metal buttons, or keys taken from another car?
why: The DCU's panel replaces the factory climate controls in the centre stack. Its nine keys (defog, hatch, fuel door, HVAC mode, recirculate, and four window keys) are yours to style. That choice fixes which switch parts are bought, how the panel board is laid out, how the keys are backlit, and how the faceplate is drawn. The knobs take the same style.
options:
(a) Factory-style: a flat faceplate with its own key caps, lettered or with symbols, pressing low-travel switches on the panel board. It is backlit from behind like a modern car's console and looks OEM. The faceplate and caps are printed or made to your drawing. It is the cheapest in switches and takes the most drawing work.
(b) Individual round metal pushbuttons (12-16 mm, each with a light ring) set into a plain plate, with metal knobs to match. It is an aftermarket or race look, about $5-12 per button, and the buttons wire to the panel board rather than soldering to it.
(c) Switches taken from another car (a modern OEM climate or console module used for its keys only). It has a finished OEM look, but only as good as the donor's layout fits nine keys and four knobs. The cost and the hunt depend on the donor.
recommend: (a), unless you want the machined aftermarket look, or already have a donor module in mind
stops: The key switch parts (electrical P155), the panel board's layout (electrical H-008) and the faceplate (LP20)
